newsitem.title: POLAND: FORECAST - Polish 1996 trade gap seen at PLN 6 bln.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Polish 1996 trade gap seen at PLN 6 bln.

text.p: Poland's trade gap increased nearly sevenfold in January-July against the same period of 1995 and could top $6 billion this year, but current account should be balanced thanks to cross-border trade inflows, analysts said.

On Friday, the central bank said Poland had a $10 million current account deficit in the January-July period, but that the merchandise trade gap ballooned to nearly $3.7 billion from some $530 million in the corresponding period of 1995.

"Poland is looking at a minimum trade deficit of $6 billion in 1996, although there are signs that exports are beginning to pick up," Tadeusz Chroscicki, head analyst at the Planning Ministry, told Reuters on Monday.
Other analysts' forecasts for the 1996 trade gap range between $5 and $7 billion after a $1.8 billion deficit in 1995.

Analysts said exports, which grew 8.2 percent in the first seven months of this year from the same period of 1995, would grow quicker in the fourth quarter of the year as the economic climate in Germany, Poland's main trading partner, warms up.
"Exports should grow by over 10 percent by the end of the year from the current 8.2 percent pace," Chroscicki said.
He said exports in July were 18 percent larger than in the same month of 1995, the largest monthly growth rate this year.
Analysts said that despite the larger merchandise trade deficit Poland's current account remained in balance because of huge unofficial cross-border trade inflows.

"Cross-border trade flows should remain fairly constant in the mid-term and continue to neutralise the huge merchandise trade deficit," said Adam Czyzewski of the independent NOBE economic think-tank.

Analysts said the quick growth rate of imports, at 32 percent in the first seven months of 1996, was not problematic for the economy because it was largely caused by rapid growth of investment and machinery imports.
"Polish imports are very often connected with investment, as is often the case in a rapidly developing economy -- which usually is a net importer of capital," Czyzewski said.

Analysts said that despite the balanced current account flows Poland's foreign currency reserves grew by $2.83 billion to $17.78 billion in the January-July period, mainly on the back of foreign direct investment (FDI) inflows.

"FDI in Poland is largely responsible for growth of the country's currency reserves, which should moderatly increase for the rest of the year," said Krzysztof Fidor, economist at the Pioneer mutual fund.
Foreigners invested some $3.4 billion in the first seven months of 1996 and the Polish Foreign Investment Agency (PAIZ) said investment should reach $4 billion by the end of the year.
